source: Sparrow, Liu, Wegner (2011) Google effects on memory
finding: Original claim: people who expect to find facts later remember the facts less and remember where to find them better. Founding empirical support for transactive memory with the internet.
numbers: Numbers not re-read this session. Small student samples.
limits: Not opened; later replications failed on the Stroop experiment.
agent_relevance: Offloading can change what the thinker stores. Expect an agent to store pointers, not content, when notes are reliable.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Replicating social-science experiments in Nature and Science 2010-2015 (Sparrow 2011 experiment)
finding: The Google Stroop experiment of Sparrow et al. did not replicate. Same direction as the original, not significant.
numbers: Round 1: p=0.2647. Rounds 1+2 pooled: p=0.4493. Outcome recorded as failed.
limits: Atlas page gives no N or effect size. Sparrow objected that computer-term stimuli were obsolete and cognitive load was manipulated differently. Only one experiment of the paper was tested.
agent_relevance: Do not build the agent on the claim that having a tool changes primed memory. The strong Google-makes-you-forget reading is not established.

source: Hesselmann (2020) No conclusive evidence for a Google Stroop effect: a replication
finding: Second replication, with materials revised after Sparrow's critique, again found no conclusive evidence of the Google Stroop effect.
numbers: No numbers read (page blocked; search snippet only).
limits: Not opened. Verdict from a search result title and snippet.
agent_relevance: Two failed replications of the flagship offloading-priming result. Treat as unreliable.

source: Meta-analysis (2024) Google effects on memory: media effects of intensive Internet search
finding: Random-effects meta-analysis finds moderate positive Google effects on cognitive load, cognitive self-esteem and behaviour, but not on cognitive measurement or psychophysiology.
numbers: 22 articles, 35 comparisons, N=30,889. Cognitive load d=0.73 [0.22,1.24]; self-esteem d=0.91 [0.23,1.59]; behavioural phenotype d=0.39 [0.16,0.61]; cognitive measurement d=0.56 [-0.15,1.28] ns; psychophysiology d=1.01 [-0.12,2.13] ns. Region moderator Q=6.20, p<.05.
limits: Overall pooled d and I2 not reported in text. Publication bias judged only by funnel plot. Effects mostly self-report; objective memory measures not significant. Moderator table inconsistent with subgroup estimates.
agent_relevance: What shifts with offloading is felt load and confidence, not measured memory. Do not count self-reported ease as evidence of better thinking.

source: Ward, Duke, Gneezy, Bos (2017) Brain drain: mere presence of one's smartphone reduces available cognitive capacity
finding: Original: phone on desk gave lower working-memory span and fluid intelligence than phone in another room; stronger for phone-dependent people.
numbers: From memory, unverified: about 800 participants over two experiments, small to medium effects.
limits: Not opened. Exact numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: A tool's mere availability might tax attention. Reason to keep the agent's tool list short.

source: Replication of Ward et al. (2017) Exp. 2, Acta Psychologica (2022)
finding: Pre-registered direct replication with six conditions (phone on desk, in pocket or bag, outside room; power on or off). The brain-drain effect did not replicate on operation span or go/no-go.
numbers: Abstract only: no difference between location conditions. N not read.
limits: Abstract from OpenAlex; full text not read.
agent_relevance: Mere presence of a tool is not shown to cost capacity.

source: Meta-analysis (2023) Does the Brain Drain Effect Really Exist?
finding: Overall significant negative effect of smartphone use and presence, but heterogeneous. Domains (memory, attention, general performance) differ, and country of origin moderates.
numbers: 22 studies, 43 effects (abstract). Pooled value not read.
limits: Abstract only (full text blocked). Pools use and presence, so not a clean test of mere presence.
agent_relevance: Costs sit with use, not presence. For an agent, cost comes from calls made, not tools listed.

source: Four-level meta-analysis (2024) Effect of mere presence of smartphone on cognitive functions
finding: A 2024 four-level meta-analysis on mere presence exists; result not read.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Title only.
agent_relevance: Check before citing brain drain as settled; the field is contested.

source: High-school classroom study (2025) Does the mere presence of smartphones impact cognition?
finding: Two school experiments found no clear evidence that a phone on the desk impairs fluid intelligence.
numbers: Study 1 n=195 (desk 96, bag 99). Study 2 n=115 (desk 41, bag 49, teacher desk 25). Some comparisons slightly favoured phones away.
limits: Abstract only. Separation anxiety is a rival explanation.
agent_relevance: Further failure to find a presence cost under realistic conditions.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT: cognitive debt
finding: Essay writing with LLM, search engine or no tool. EEG connectivity scaled down with external support. LLM users quoted their own essays worse and felt less ownership.
numbers: 54 people in sessions 1-3 (18 per group), 18 in session 4. Session 1: 15/18 (83.3%) LLM users could not give a correct quote vs 2/18 (11.1%) in search and brain-only; p<.001 both. Session 4: LLM-to-Brain showed weaker alpha and beta connectivity; Brain-to-LLM higher connectivity.
quote: LLM users consistently underperformed at neural, linguistic, and behavioral levels.
limits: Small N, preprint, EEG statistics poorly specified (see next line). Task engagement may explain the pattern.
agent_relevance: If the agent offloads writing to a tool, it may not hold the content. Make it reread or quote notes before relying on them.

source: Stankovic et al. (2026) Comment on Your Brain on ChatGPT
finding: Critique of the Kosmyna study: low power, reporting inconsistencies, unclear EEG statistics, overinterpretation, and practice effects in session 4.
numbers: States 55 participants completed but only 54 analysed. FDR correction mentioned only for some comparisons. ANOVA results not reported. Quote-correctness criteria unexplained.
limits: Comment, not a replication. No new data.
agent_relevance: Treat the LLM cognitive-debt EEG claim as a hypothesis. The quoting result is behavioural and simpler, but still a small sample.

source: Maier, Schwabe, Schneider, Feuerriegel (2026) Designing against deskilling
finding: Preregistered online RCT: practising fraction arithmetic with an LLM that gives answers on request. Plain LLM access did not significantly lower unaided test scores. Metacognitive feedback reduced offloading and raised test score; an effort reward did nothing.
numbers: N=704, five conditions. Control unaided 0.65 vs AI-only 0.62, OR 0.80 [0.42,1.51], p=.244 (H1 not supported). Metacognitive feedback: offloading OR=0.47, test OR=1.51. Exploratory: +10 points of answer offloading gave OR=0.68 [0.62,0.74] on test items (558 people, 3,348 items).
limits: Online UK adults, short task, one-sided tests. Offloading-test link is correlational.
agent_relevance: Tool use hurts later unaided skill only when the tool does the work. Show the agent the cost of handing off and gate answer-offloading, not tool access.

source: Shen and Tamkin (2026) How AI impacts skill formation
finding: Randomised trial: developers learning a new async Python library with or without an AI assistant. AI group scored lower on a knowledge quiz with no reliable speed gain. Interaction pattern mattered: delegation hurt, conceptual questions did not.
numbers: Main study n=52 (26 per arm). Quiz Cohen d=0.738, p=0.01. Pilot D: AI faster (d=1.11, p=0.03) and quiz worse. Patterns: conceptual inquiry about 65% quiz, AI delegation about 39%, iterative AI debugging about 24%.
limits: Small N, GPT-4o, one library, 35-minute limit. Pilots had 35% non-compliance with the no-AI rule. Pattern comparison is non-randomised.
agent_relevance: Delegation versus inquiry is a real moderator. Use notes and tools as scaffolds for reasoning, and keep derivation inside the agent's own steps.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS
finding: RCT in a Turkish high school: students with plain GPT-4 did better in practice but worse on later unaided exams. A tutor version with safeguards largely removed the harm.
numbers: Nearly 1,000 students (search snippet). Preprint reported 17% worse for GPT Base; not verified in the final paper.
limits: Not opened (PNAS blocked). Single school, fall 2023.
agent_relevance: Guardrails on the tool (hints, not answers) keep the benefit. Fits the schema rule that code, not the model, controls what the tool gives.

source: Klett and Ahle (2024) Extended Mind Transformers
finding: Retrieval of key-value memories inside attention. Needs retrieval in most decoder layers. Beats fine-tuned long-context models on a counterfactual retrieval benchmark, by 6% on average.
numbers: Perplexity stays stable at lengths where a naive baseline blows up (one table cell 49.7). Counterfactual retrieval accuracy roughly 33-43% at 2k-16k for baselines; 43-59% with RAG. Combined with RAG beat GPT-4 by 6%.
limits: Name borrows from Clark and Chalmers; no test of the philosophical claim. Benchmark is new and from the authors. Table layout hard to read from text extraction.
agent_relevance: Memory outside the context can be read as if inside. Supports external notes consulted at each step.

source: An (2025) Cognitive Workspace: active memory management for LLMs
finding: Proposes active, task-driven external memory instead of passive RAG, citing Clark's extended mind thesis. Reports a high memory reuse rate and a net efficiency gain.
numbers: Average reuse 58.6% (54-60%) vs 0% for RAG; net efficiency gain 17-18% with 3.3x more operations; Cohen's d about 190. Test corpus: 8 AI documents.
limits: Metrics are counted operations, not task accuracy. Cohen's d near 190 signals a deterministic baseline, so the statistics are not meaningful. Single author, tiny corpus.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Keeping and reusing working state is plausible but not proven by this paper.

source: Packer et al. (2023) MemGPT: LLMs as operating systems
finding: A model that pages its own memory between context and external storage using function calls. Large gains on deep-memory retrieval over fixed-context baselines.
numbers: Deep memory retrieval accuracy: GPT-3.5 Turbo 38.7% to 66.9%; GPT-4 32.1% to 92.5%; GPT-4 Turbo 35.3% to 93.4% with MemGPT. Nested key-value retrieval: fixed-context baselines fall toward 0% with deeper nesting.
limits: Tasks built or adapted by the authors. Retrieval quality limits the document-QA arm.
agent_relevance: Direct test that an external store, managed by the thinker, extends effective memory. Supports notes plus code-controlled retrieval.

source: Yao et al. (2023) ReAct: reasoning and acting
finding: Interleaving reasoning with tool actions grounds answers. Tool access alone (Act) is much worse than tool plus reasoning on ALFWorld.
numbers: ALFWorld success: ReAct best 71%, Act best 45%, BUTLER 37%; relative gain over Act 33-90%, mean 62%. HotpotQA: CoT-SC to ReAct 34.2, ReAct to CoT-SC 35.1 (best). Failure analysis: CoT hallucination 56% of failures vs ReAct 0%; ReAct reasoning error 47%, search-result error 23%.
limits: Few-shot prompting, small benchmarks, older models. On HotpotQA ReAct alone is not better than CoT.
agent_relevance: The extended system is the loop of thought plus lookup. A tool without a reasoning trace loses the thread. Combine with fallback to internal reasoning.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Verbal reflections stored in an external episodic buffer improve later attempts. Reflection adds value beyond storing past trajectories.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91%. Gains over baselines: +22% ALFWorld (12 steps), +20% HotpotQA, +11% HumanEval. Reflection adds 8% absolute over episodic-memory-only. ReAct-only agent stays at 22% hallucination rate.
limits: Relies on a signal (test pass or fail, environment reward). Without a reliable signal reflections may mislead.
agent_relevance: External memory helps most when it stores a distilled lesson linked to real feedback (guardrail G2).

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager
finding: Agent with an external skill library of executable code and a curriculum. Removing the skill library makes progress plateau.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x the best baseline. GPT-4 gives 5.7x more unique items than GPT-3.5. Without the skill library the agent plateaus in later stages. Other ablations remove feedback, execution errors, self-verification.
limits: One game, three runs per method. Gains come from several components together.
agent_relevance: External code as stored skill is a measured extension of capability. Skills must be verified before storing (G3).

source: Schick et al. (2023) Toolformer
finding: A model taught to call calculator, search, calendar and other tools improves zero-shot performance, beating a much larger GPT-3 (175B) on several tasks.
numbers: Per-task figures not recorded this session.
limits: Self-supervised tool use, 2023 models, inline calls.
agent_relevance: Tool use can substitute for scale on facts and arithmetic.

source: Clark and Chalmers (1998) The extended mind
finding: Parity principle and Otto's notebook: reliable, accessible, trusted external stores can count as part of memory.
numbers: No empirical numbers; conceptual argument.
limits: Not opened. Critics (Adams and Aizawa) say causal coupling does not show constitution.
agent_relevance: The agent's notes can be treated as memory if always available, trusted, and consulted automatically. Those are the tests to meet.

source: Risko and Gilbert (2016) Cognitive offloading
finding: Review: people offload by metacognitive cost-benefit judgement. Offloading frees capacity but can reduce memory for offloaded items. Choice depends on confidence in own memory.
numbers: No numbers recorded this session.
limits: Not opened. Cited from memory.
agent_relevance: When to offload is a metacognitive decision; in our design it belongs to code, not the model.

source: Storm and Stone (2015); Henkel (2014) offloading and photo-taking
finding: Saving a file freed capacity to learn new material (Storm and Stone). Photographing museum objects lowered later memory for them (Henkel 2014). Offloading has both a benefit and a cost.
numbers: From memory, unverified; not recorded.
limits: Not opened. Photo-taking impairment has mixed follow-ups.
agent_relevance: Saved material can free budget for new work, but the agent must still look at what it saved.

source: Synthesis across b02, b04, b11, b12 (angle B)
finding: What holds up: the original Google-memory result and the smartphone-presence result are weak. Stronger evidence is later-skill harm when the tool does the task (delegation), and gains when external memory is actively managed.
limits: Synthesis by this agent; not an independent source.
agent_relevance: Design on delegation versus engagement, not on mere availability.
